fatal_errors: The proposed sub-Tg anneal does not reconstruct the demonstrated intervention, which was changing the Fe/Co/Mn/P composition followed by melt spinning at 40 m/s.
No glass transition was detected in the reported alloy, so a sub-Tg hold and a Tg-Tx stability interval cannot be operationally defined from the available thermal data.
A post-quench hold cannot increase the amorphous fraction already retained during quenching; it may instead promote structural relaxation, nucleation, or partial crystallization.
The hypothesis omits the demonstrated processing boundaries of approximately 20 micrometer ribbons, 40 m/s wheel speed, and DSC reheating at 20 K/min.
No prior evidence is cited to support the claimed suppression of nucleation by sub-Tg relaxation.
explanation: The response recognizes the general goals of amorphous retention and delayed crystallization, but it proposes a different and unsupported intervention. The target result arose from reducing P from 20 to 15 at.% and adjusting Fe, Co, and Mn to favor eutectic-dominated solidification, combined with sufficiently rapid melt spinning to suppress segregation and phosphide nucleation. The generated mechanism is questionable because sub-Tg relaxation does not generally remove heterogeneous nucleation sites and can increase kinetic susceptibility to crystallization. Its baseline also conflates primary crystallization during cooling with multistage devitrification during reheating. The paired DSC/XRD experiment is directionally useful, but reduced exotherm area is ambiguous because it could indicate crystallization during the hold rather than improved stability, and Tg-Tx is inappropriate where Tg is undetected. Pre- and post-hold phase quantification plus isothermal calorimetry or microscopy would be needed for decisive discrimination.
